clue.text: Reaction to a birching?

parts.note: a hostile reaction, pictured literally as the lash of the birch that lands on the culprit's back

explanation.surface: What follows when a schoolboy is given the birch.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the word for a strong adverse reaction can be split into the place a birch lands and the stroke it deals.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp adverse response to some event or policy is the everyday sense; a flogging is the literal picture.

clue.text: Bill makes a statement:

definitions.meaning: a narrative report or description of events

explanation.surface: A piece of legislation announces something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an invoice of charges and also a narrative description or report.

clue.text: Ruler dashes off for machinery parts

parts.note: a king is a ruler
to bolt is to dash off, run away

explanation.surface: A monarch hurries away to buy spare components.
explanation.definitionFit: Large vertical pins that act as pivots, for example joining a carriage body to its front axle.

clue.text: Archbishop confuses fifty names

indicators.note: confuses means the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A senior cleric muddles up a list of fifty names.
explanation.definitionFit: St Anselm was an eleventh-century Archbishop of Canterbury and theologian.

clue.text: Old hero-he gets his guerdon for watchfulness ?

parts.note: taken as written
guerdon is an archaic word for a reward
the epithet 'the Wake' is traditionally said to mean 'the watchful one', a wake being a vigil

explanation.surface: An ancient champion receives a prize for staying alert.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereward the Wake was an English outlaw who led resistance to William the Conqueror in the Fens; his byname is usually glossed as 'the watchful'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eleventh-century English rebel leader, celebrated in legend and in Charles Kingsley's novel.

clue.text: He's better at pushing the boat out

definitions.text: He's better at pushing the boat out

parts.words: He's better at pushing the boat out
parts.note: one who places bets (a 'better') and also one who pushes a flat boat along with a pole

explanation.surface: A man who is more skilled at launching boats, or one who spends lavishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is one who bets, not a comparison, and 'pushing the boat out' (spending freely) is also literally poling a flat river boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a gambler placing a wager and a person propelling a flat-bottomed river craft with a pole.

clue.text: Shut up one tent: sorry !

parts.note: to pen an animal is to shut it up in an enclosure
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Confined to a single tent, someone feels regretful.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling remorse for wrongdoing, contrite.

clue.text: Art upset Benito ? Slander !

indicators.note: upset means the letters of art are knocked over into a new order

parts.note: Benito Mussolini was styled Il Duce, the leader

explanation.surface: An artwork offended Mussolini, who calls it defamatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ART into TRA; Benito Mussolini, Italy's fascist dictator, was known as Il Duce.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak maliciously and falsely about someone, to defame.

clue.text: Staggered about etc., maybe, but was given his old seat

indicators.note: about means the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: to reel is to stagger, so staggered gives reeled

indicators.note: maybe signals that the letters given may be in another order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the abbreviation as written

explanation.surface: A drunk lurched around before his party gave him back his place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges ETC to ECT, and 'about' puts REELED round it, after REEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An MP voted back in at an election regains the constituency held before.

clue.text: They count as part of the act

definitions.text: They count as part of the act

parts.words: They count as part of the act
parts.note: a stage play's act is divided into smaller sections, each a unit of action

explanation.surface: Things that are included in a performer's routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The act' suggests a variety turn, but it is a division of a play, which is made up of smaller sections.
explanation.definitionFit: In drama an act is subdivided into episodes of continuous action in one setting.

clue.text: The vagabond will smuggle a gem

parts.note: to run goods is to smuggle them, as in gun-running
an agate is a banded semi-precious stone; with the A it gives the gem, the clue's 'a' supplying its first letter

explanation.surface: A tramp intends to sneak a jewel past customs.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a wanderer or fugitive, a roving person with no fixed home.

clue.text: Pleated border with mink underneath ?

parts.note: mink is a kind of fur
underneath means below

explanation.surface: A dress hem trimmed with mink along its lower edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounce, a gathered or pleated strip trimming a skirt or petticoat.

clue.text: A single treble, Trinity type

definitions.meaning: one thing that is also threefold, three in one
of the kind of the Christian Trinity, three persons in one God

explanation.surface: One high-voice chorister from Trinity College.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means three in one, the character of the Holy Trinity, so it is both one and threefold.

clue.text: Moonshine in this part of the night?

definitions.meaning: illicit spirit, moonshine, is made in a distilling apparatus
the silent hush of the night, as in 'the dead of night'

explanation.surface: Bootleg liquor drunk in the small hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moonshine' is not moonlight but bootleg spirit, made in a distilling apparatus; the other sense is the quiet of the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A still is the apparatus that distils illicit liquor, and 'the still of the night' is its hushed calm.

clue.text: Not quick time, though the month includes some that is fast

definitions.text: Not quick time, though the month includes some that is fast

parts.words: Not quick time, though the month includes some that is fast
parts.note: a military pace opposite to quick time, named as if the third month of the year were slow, though part of the Lenten fast falls in it

explanation.surface: A ponderous period, even though it contains some days of fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: In drill, quick time is the brisk pace; the other is a solemn pace. The third month usually contains part of Lent, a fast, so it is not wholly slow.
explanation.definitionFit: A deliberate ceremonial marching pace, used at funerals, in contrast to the normal quick step.

clue.text: Passing rains broke into tent

indicators.note: the reworked letters go into the word tent, splitting it open

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: rains broke means the letters of rains are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Rain burst through the canvas of a campsite shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' turns RAINS into RANSI, and 'into' puts that inside TENT, after its first T.
explanation.definitionFit: Something brief or fleeting is passing, staying only a short time.

clue.text: Resulting in Father Brown's acquittal ?

parts.note: the title of G. K. Chesterton's first book of stories about his priest-detective, read as the verdict of a trial

explanation.surface: The reason Chesterton's priest was cleared in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Brown is G. K. Chesterton's priest-detective; his first collection's title, read literally, is what an acquittal declares.
explanation.definitionFit: Freedom from guilt is what a not-guilty verdict establishes.

clue.text: Mistral maiden weighs anchor?

definitions.note: the definition describes what the machine does rather than naming it, a noun described by its action

parts.note: the mistral is a cold wind of southern France
a lass is a girl or maiden

explanation.surface: A girl from Provence sets sail as the cold wind blows.
explanation.walkthrough: The mistral is a wind; the definition is by example of what the device does, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A winch with a horizontal drum, on a ship used to haul up the anchor cable.

clue.text: Fringes with female garments no longer fashionable

parts.note: a style that is out has gone out of fashion
skirts are garments worn by women

explanation.surface: Dated women's clothing trimmed with fringes.
explanation.definitionFit: The edges or margins of a place, especially a town's border areas.

clue.text: Hot air from the Sandhurst pupil

parts.note: taken as written
RMA is the Royal Military Academy, at Sandhurst in England
L stands for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Pompous talk from a young army cadet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot air' suggests empty talk but means a rising current of warm air.
explanation.definitionFit: A column of warm rising air, used by gliders and birds to gain height.

clue.text: Massage is a necessity, one hears

indicators.note: these words signal that the word for necessity is to be taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a necessity is a need

explanation.surface: A rubdown is something everyone requires.
explanation.definitionFit: To work muscles with the hands, pressing and squeezing, as in a rubdown.

clue.text: Get the point of serving Harry salt

parts.note: in tennis an ace is a serve that wins the point outright
Harry Tate was a famous English music-hall comedian

explanation.surface: Understand why one should offer Harry the salt cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Tate was a British music-hall comic of the early twentieth century; 'salt' is the chemist's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A compound formed from acetic acid, chemically classed with sodium chloride as a salt.

clue.text: Make a start, but transpose to this form of printing

indicators.note: transpose means the two halves of the phrase change places

parts.note: to set off is to make a start on a journey

explanation.surface: Begin, then switch to a different printing process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transpose' swaps the two parts of SET OFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithography in which ink is transferred from plate to a rubber blanket and then onto paper.

clue.text: She made an uncommonly wild reveller

indicators.note: uncommonly means the letters appear in an unusual arrangement, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman created an exceptionally riotous party guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' looks as if it qualifies 'wild', but it rearranges MADE AN.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a frenzied female follower of Dionysus, a byword for a frenzied woman at revels.

clue.text: Result Edward accomplished

parts.note: a result is an effect
Ed is the short form of Edward

explanation.surface: The outcome Edward brought about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Result' looks like a verb but it is a noun giving the word for an outcome; 'accomplished' means brought about.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something about is to carry it out, so the past form means achieved.

clue.text: Academician may add articles on Sanskrit epic

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
taken as written
an and a are the two indefinite articles
the second of the two articles

explanation.surface: A painter of the Royal Academy might write commentary on an Indian classic.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Indian epic poem recounting the deeds of Rama, written in the classical language of India.

clue.text: Rowlandson's academic grammar

definitions.meaning: Dr ..., the schoolmaster hero of Thomas Rowlandson's comic drawings with verses by William Combe
the rules governing how words are arranged into sentences

explanation.surface: The university scholar drawn by Rowlandson teaches language rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Rowlandson was an English caricaturist whose Tours of Dr Syntax followed a pedantic clergyman-schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Syntax is the cartoonist's pedant, and the word itself is the part of grammar dealing with sentence structure.

clue.text: Shares the hole with football players

definitions.meaning: in golf, to tie a hole with the opponent by taking the same number of strokes
half-backs, players positioned between forwards and defenders

explanation.surface: A golfer splits a hole while playing alongside some footballers.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf a hole is halved when both sides take the same score; in older football line-ups the half-backs were called by this short name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tying a golf hole is the verb sense; midfield players in old football formations are the noun sense.

clue.text: It's too far to go to these remotest parts

definitions.text: It's too far to go to these
definitions.meaning: the idiom of going to excessive lengths, overdoing things
the outermost limits or furthest points

explanation.surface: A journey to the far ends of the earth is too long to make.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to such lengths is to act excessively, and the noun also means the farthest boundaries.
